awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: Efficient Thermal-Spatial Point-Cloud Extraction and Rapid Assessment of Physics-Based AI Algorithm from Infrared Images to Increase Early Detection of Breast Cancer
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project relates to improving women’s health through early detection of breast cancer. Women above age of 40 years are advised to undergo annual/biannual screening for breast cancer. In the current breast cancer screening paradigm, mammography is supplemented by adjunctive technologies, such as ultrasound imaging, to improve the cancer detection rates. However, shortcomings from imaging dense breast tissue relating to higher patient recall rates for additional screening and lower detection accuracy have impacted confidence in screening. This SBIR Phase I project aims to improve early cancer detection by providing an innovative screening tool that can accurately detect breast cancer, even in dense breasts. The increase in the overall detection rates and improved cancer detection from this screening tool is expected to provide significant short-term and long-term savings in healthcare costs. This technology is cost-effective as it does not require skilled technologists screening patients. It will increase the revenue to hospitals/breast clinics while providing more confidence in cancer screening and saving out of pocket expense to patients.

This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project addresses a critical societal need for accurate breast cancer detection, especially in women with dense breasts. Malignant tumors generate more heat as compared to healthy tissue due to their increased metabolic activity. It changes the heat signature on the surface of the breast that can be captured by an infrared camera. This concept was utilized to develop a device that can extract the surface temperatures of the using infrared imaging. A physics-based artificial intelligence (AI) algorithm then back-calculates the size and location of a malignant tumor from these surface temperatures. The technology is free from harmful radiations and is contactless. To meet current clinical workflow demands, improvements in imaging and computing times will be pursued through technical research. Further research in data generation from imaging and physics-based AI techniques will be conducted to reduce the imaging and computing times to integrate this technology into clinical settings. An Institutional Review Board approved clinical study will be undertaken to validate the methods developed in this project. The outcome from this project will be a rapid breast cancer screening technology that will meet current clinical demands for early detection of cancer.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This NSF SBIR Phase I project aided the development of a novel adjunctive breast cancer screening technology that overcomes major hurdles in the current screening paradigm which misses about 30% of cancers due to the difficulty of imaging dense breast tissue. Adjunctive screening to mammography helps somewhat improve the detection rate, but also increases false positive cases. This increase in false positive cases has led to an increase in unnecessary biopsies and a decrease in patient confidence in the current screening paradigm. Many patients go through tremendous turmoil throughout the screening process that requires them to be recalled and have follow-ups due to their dense tissue. BiRed Imaging has developed a thermophysics-based adjunctive breast cancer screening technology to help address this problem and improve the current paradigm. The core concept of this technology uses the fact that malignant tumors have a substantially high metabolic heat generation rate and associated blood perfusion network. This core concept was validated in 2020 with 24 biopsy-proven patients during a previous Institutional Review Board (IRB) approved clinical study at Rochester General Hospital (RGH). The technology was able to accurately detect the presence and absence of breast cancer regardless of breast tissue density.

During a previous Phase I project, an imaging device prototype was fabricated, and both a 3D temperature extraction and physics-based AI algorithms were developed. The device takes multi-view infrared (IR) and optical images of the breast in the prone position. The extraction algorithm generates 3D data with corresponding temperatures using the images and provides them to the AI algorithm to solve bioheat equations and detect tumor heat source. The fabrication of the prototype and development of the algorithms allowed for a transition from exploratory research to research and development (R&D). During the current Phase I project, further R&D efforts were conducted to move this technology towards commercialization. The goals of the current Phase I project were: (i) enhance the technology to meet clinical needs and (ii) validate the prototype and algorithms with clinical data. The first goal was achieved through the reduction in image capture time  to 15 minutes and the compute time of the AI-based detection algorithm to 10 minutes. The second goal was achieved through a new IRB-approved clinical study at RGH for clinical validation with 15 new patients.

For the first goal, new software was developed to inform the technician when the patient’s breast has acclimated and is ready for imaging. Previously, the technician had to wait for about 10 minutes per breast to ensure that each breast has adjusted to the room temperature, also known as acclimation. The total time for imaging a patient was about 32 minutes, or about 16 minutes per breast, with acclimation taking up 20 minutes of the total time. The new software showed that acclimation can be reached within 5-6 minutes, reducing the total time by 10 minutes. After obtaining feedback from patients and technicians during the clinical study, BiRed is working with a contract manufacturer on the next generation imaging device prototype. The new device will be able image patients in less than 15 minutes, which rivals that of other adjunct imaging modalities. Additionally, BiRed is working on designing this device to meet the comfort needs of the patients to provide the best quality of care.

BiRed has made major innovative strides in the fields of physics-based AI and bioheat transfer to reduce the compute time of the AI. Through the work completed in this Phase I project, enhancements and AI-based novel approaches reduced the compute time from over 90 hours to 10 minutes per breast. This shows the potential of providing clinicians with results withing minutes after imaging. Towards the end of the project, the research algorithms were packaged into a software module. This shows the ability of BiRed to conduct impactful R&D work and to begin transition towards product development and commercialization. The second goal showed that this technology is both efficient and accurate in obtaining results. The technology was validated with 15 patients prior to their biopsy with results showing no cancers missed and no false positives regardless of breast tissue density. These results have been encouraging and has shown the need for larger studies to validate the efficacy of the technology. Having accurate results also encourages patients to trust the screening process. Since this technology is non-invasive, contactless and radiation-free, it provides a safe and comfortable option for patients.

Overall, the outcomes of this project have shown the potential of taking this technology to the adjunct breast cancer screening marking. The BiRed technology shows the potential to meet clinical demands while providing an accurate and fast screening modality that is safe and comfortable for patients. The advancement of this technology has led to innovative leaps and scientific contributions in the fields of imaging, bioheat transfer and physics-based AI.
